Crash Pad
KRASH pad
noun (Boomer slang)
Crash (to sleep, slang) + pad (one’s bed or lodging, 1930s jazz slang, from the older sense of a bundle of straw to lie on). A crash pad — an apartment or house where anyone could sleep for free, often on mattresses covering the floor — was a fixture of the mid-1960s counterculture, especially in Haight-Ashbury and the East Village during 1966–68, when runaways poured into both. Airline crews later used crash pad for a shared apartment near a base.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A crash pad was a hippie flophouse: an apartment where anyone could sleep, mattresses wall to wall, the door always open. In 1967 there were hundreds in San Francisco and New York, filled with runaways, drifters, and the predators who followed them. The Christian observation: the crash pad was a counterfeit of something God intends — a home for the homeless — built without the one thing that makes a home safe. Scripture says, "God setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6). The young people who flocked to the crash pads had often fled real families, some of them cruel, and were looking for belonging. What they found instead was a room without a father: no one in charge, no one responsible, no protection for the weak. Proverbs saw the danger: "As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place" (Pro 27:8), and "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners" (1Co 15:33). The story that fits is the prodigal’s. In the far country, with the crash-pad friends gone, "when he came to himself, he said ... I will arise and go to my father" (Luk 15:17–18). The Christian answer to the crash pad is not a locked door but a household with a father in it — a church and a home with room at the table, where "the solitary" are set "in families" and the lost can come home.

Webster 1828 Definition

Mid-1960s counterculture slang for a communal apartment where anyone could sleep free — a counterfeit home without a father, answered by the God who setteth the solitary in families (Psa 68:6).

expand to see more

CRASH PAD, n. (Boomer slang, mid-1960s) A house or apartment providing free, temporary sleeping space, typically on floor mattresses, for transients and runaways; hence any place to stay temporarily. Later, a shared lodging for airline crews.

Webster (1828) — PAD, noun A soft saddle, cushion or bolster stuffed with straw, hair or other soft substance.

Pad (1930s jazz slang) — one’s bed or home (see Pad).

Modern Corruption

The crash pad offered belonging without authority and shelter without protection; Scripture’s answer is the household with a father in it, where God sets the solitary in families.

expand to see more

The crash pad was idealistic: share everything, own nothing, welcome all. It failed for the reason every fatherless arrangement fails. Without anyone responsible, the strongest took what they wanted and the weakest paid. Reports from the Haight in 1967 tell of runaway girls exploited within days of arriving, of hepatitis and malnutrition, of drugs pushed on children. Belonging without authority is not freedom; it is exposure.

The church has a better answer and has not always given it. The prodigals of 1967 needed doors that were open and houses that were ordered — love and law together. That is what a Christian home is meant to be, and what a congregation is meant to be for those who have no home. God "setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6), and He does it, very often, through families who have made room.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Crash (slang, to sleep) + pad (1930s jazz, a bed or home; from pad, a bundle of straw) → mid-1960s crash pad, Haight-Ashbury and East Village.

expand to see more

Pad — 16th c., a bundle of straw to lie on; 1930s jazz slang, one’s bed or lodging

Crash — slang, to sleep somewhere temporary

1966–68: crash pads in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury and New York’s East Village

Later: airline-crew crash pads near hub airports

Scripture: Psa 68:6 — the solitary set in families
